newsitem.title: CHINA: HK property supply picture little changed - analysts.
newsitem.headline: HK property supply picture little changed - analysts.

text.p: Hong Kong's planS to boost housing supply will do little to change the dynamics of the territory's booming property market, where demand should continue to outstrip supply, analysts said on Wednesday.
"I think based on this sales programme, the actual supply in prospective years will still fall short of demand," said Edward Chan, head of research at Amsteel Securities.
"Even when the government says they are actually going to sell more land over the next five years, it will not come to the market for at least another 24 months," he added.
Hong Kong's new government announced on Tuesday that it would sell a total 433 hectares of land over the next five years, up 140 percent compared with the previous five years.

In the first 21-month phase of the two-part land disposal programme -- from July 1, 1997 to March 31, 1999 -- a total 157.24 hectares of land, estimated to yield 64,762 new residential units, would be sold, it said.
Michael Leary, senior property analyst at Lehman Brothers, said he still expected to see 10 percent growth in real estate prices in each of 1997 and 1998.
"We are only looking at total supply of around 65,000 units in 1998, up from about 60,000 in 1997, and we have got a projection of 84,000 for 1999," he said.
"Demand will be about 85,000 a year so you have still got a case of meaningful mismatch here for the next few years which will continue to drive pressure on price upwards."
While the government has vowed to increase the supply of public housing, analysts said private developers would have to be encouraged to increase supply.

"The problem remains for the government as how does it encourage developers to produce more volume. Their primary concern is aimed very much at sustainable earnings growth," said Andrew Taylor, property analyst at Paribas Asia Equity.

But analysts said real estate prices, which have risen 30 percent this year, were likely to soften over coming months due to uncertainty surrounding the contents of a much-awaited policy statement by the government in October.
Fears of measures to curb speculative activity have already reduced transactions in the property market, they said.
Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd only sold 80 percent of the flats it had on offer at its Grand Del Sol development in the New Territories on the first sale day on last Saturday.
Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd priced flats at its Vista Paradiso project in the New Territories below market expectations last week.

"Cheung Kong reduced its prices of Vista Paradiso which created a certain containing effect in the property market," said Chan. "What we have heard is that asking prices in the New Territories and certain luxury areas have fallen by about five percent since Cheung Kong announced Vista Paridiso prices."
Leary said property prices could decline by about five percent in the third quarter.
Chan saw a 10 percent decline in property prices during the second half of 1997. "However, it is not good enough to restore affordability to historically normal levels," he said.
Chan said property stocks were likely to underperform during the second half of the year, plagued by market uncertainty.

"Short term, certainly on stock prices, it is going to have a bit of a negative effect but as people start to digest the numbers, people will realise the stocks have been oversold," said Taylor. "You are really looking at a supply scenario which is not really any different."
